body:
### The idea in one or two sentences

We infer the hidden dependency graph in a GitHub backlog, determining what blocks what, and write it into GitHub's native issue-dependency fields, and then serves the resulting schedule to coding agents. 

### What problem does it solve?

When agents work on issues, they usually work on them sequentially and sometimes do valid work in the wrong order, leading them to repeatedly re-derive the same dependency graph. 

We fix this by automatically inferring dependencies between issues, creating a visual dependency graph that allows agents to work in parallel on non-dependent issues, and in the correct order allowing agents to run longer on more at once without reevaluating on what to do next, as a clear path is being shown. 

### Theme (optional)

Agentic workflows (Copilot coding agent, AI-assisted planning and triage)

### Where does the "agentic" part come in?

Agents infer dependencies across the backlog from the issue text. A human reviews those proposals before anything is committed, with the agent surfacing conflicts like cycles for resolution. The approved graph then becomes the execution layer for agents: it exposes ready work, prevents parallel agents from colliding, and gives each agent the dependency context it needs to work in the right order.

### Rough effort

M — one hackathon day

### Are you planning to build this yourself?

Yes — my team is claiming it

### Team name

Pending HR Approval

### Anything else?

_No response_

### Before you submit

- [x] I searched [existing ideas](https://github.com/reneexeener/msft-hackathon-2026/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22type%3A+idea%22) and this isn't a duplicate (if it's close to another idea, link it — that's useful too).
- [x] I understand this idea is visible to every hackathon participant, and another team may build it if I don't claim it.
title: [Idea] AI Issue Orchestrator

body:
> [!NOTE]
> **Example submission, seeded by the organizers.** This is what a finished submission looks like — it's fictional, and the links don't go anywhere. Please don't edit it; [submit your own project](../../issues/new?template=2-project-submission.yml) when you're ready.

### Team name

Team Example (organizers)

### Team members

@example-one, @example-two, @example-three

### Which idea did you build?

#4

### What did you build?

**Splitter** — comment `/split` on a large issue and it comes back with a proposed breakdown into sub-issues, each tagged as *mechanical* or *judgement*. Approve the breakdown and it creates the sub-issues, links them under the parent, adds them to the board, and assigns the mechanical ones to the Copilot coding agent.

The point isn't the decomposition. Plenty of tools will chop up a ticket. The point is the **routing**: the board becomes the place where work is dispatched between people and agents, and you can see at a glance which is which.

### Theme

Automation (Actions, webhooks, bots, the GraphQL API)

### Code repository

https://github.com/example-team/splitter *(not a real link)*

### Demo link

https://youtu.be/example *(not a real link — 3 min walkthrough)*

### How did agents do the work?

Two agents, doing quite different jobs.

**Inside the product.** A model reads the parent issue plus the files it references and proposes 3–8 sub-issues, each classified mechanical or judgement. Mechanical means the outcome is fully determined by the description and a diff can be checked without an opinion. We deliberately biased the classifier toward "judgement" — a false *mechanical* produces a confident wrong PR, while a false *judgement* just means a human does something an agent could have. Those costs aren't symmetric, and pretending they were cost us most of Saturday.

Nothing is created until a human clicks approve. We tried auto-create-with-undo first. It was worse: reviewing 8 issues that already exist is meaningfully harder than reviewing 8 that don't, because deleting things feels expensive.

**Building it.** We ran Splitter on itself from Saturday lunchtime. Of 34 sub-issues it generated for our own work, 11 went to the coding agent — mostly test scaffolding, type definitions, and the GraphQL client. 9 merged with no changes, 2 needed rework. That's the honest number, and it's roughly what we'd expect from a junior teammate on unfamiliar code.

### How did your team plan and track the work?

We ran everything on this repo's board so it'd be inspectable.

One parent issue per capability (parse, classify, create, assign), sub-issues under each, and the **Team** field set so we could group the board by owner and spot pile-ups. Effort estimates were mostly wrong, which we expected, but the *shape* of the wrongness was useful: everything touching the GraphQL API took about twice what we guessed, and everything model-facing took about half.

The mid-hackathon change: we started with a Status column per capability and it was useless by Saturday afternoon — a card in "classify" told you nothing about whether it was blocked. We collapsed to the standard flow and moved capability onto a field instead, so it became a grouping rather than a position. Should have started there.

We also added a `blocked-on-human` label around hour 20, once it became clear the interesting queue wasn't "what's in progress" but "what's waiting on one of us to look at it."

### What surprised you?

**The bottleneck moved, it didn't disappear.** We assumed agent throughput was the constraint. It wasn't — the constraint became *our* review capacity. Three of us couldn't keep up with the PRs one coding agent produced, and by Sunday morning we had a queue of merged-but-unreviewed work, which is exactly the thing you're supposed to avoid. If we did it again the first feature would be a review budget, not a faster agent.

**Estimates got weirder, not better.** With a human doing the work, an S/M/L estimate is a guess about effort. With an agent, it's a guess about *how likely the agent is to get it right first time* — a totally different quantity wearing the same label. We don't think S/M/L survives contact with mixed teams, and we don't know what replaces it.

**The classifier's mistakes were legible.** We'd braced for weird ones. In practice every misclassification was a case where the issue text genuinely was ambiguous, and a human reading it would have made the same call. That was reassuring, and it also means the real lever is issue quality — which is basically idea #3, so those two should probably have been one project.

**What we'd redo:** start with the review pipeline, cap generated sub-issues sooner (our first run on a vague epic produced 22 and we lost an hour reading them), and set the Team field from the beginning instead of backfilling it on Sunday.
title: [Submission] Team Example — Splitter

> [!NOTE]
> **Example issue, seeded by the organizers.** It shows roughly the level of detail we're hoping for — yours can be shorter. Please don't edit or claim this one; [submit your own idea](../../issues/new?template=1-challenge-idea.yml) instead.

### The idea in one or two sentences

A matchmaker for newcomers: tell it roughly what you know, and it finds the handful of open issues you could genuinely finish this week — then writes the ramp-up notes needed to actually start on one.

### What problem does it solve?

`good first issue` is a label that lies. It gets applied once, usually by someone who already understands the codebase, and then never revisited — so the list fills up with issues that are stale, already half-solved in a linked PR, or "easy" only if you happen to know which of the six services owns the behaviour.

A newcomer opens that list, picks something, spends two evenings working out where the code even lives, and doesn't come back. The failure isn't difficulty. It's that the issue assumes context nobody wrote down.

### Theme

Onboarding & docs (getting new contributors productive fast)

### Where does the "agentic" part come in?

The agent does the work the label was pretending to do.

**Matching.** Given a short self-description ("comfortable with Python, never touched CI"), it reads open issues *and the code they'd touch*, then ranks them by real fit rather than by label. Crucially it can also rule things out: an issue tagged good-first-issue that turns out to need database migration knowledge gets filtered out with a reason.

**Ramp-up.** For a chosen issue it generates a starting note — which files are involved, how to run the relevant tests, which past PR is the closest precedent, and what "done" looks like. That's the two evenings it gives back.

**Staying honest.** On a schedule, it re-checks existing `good first issue` labels and flags ones that have gone stale: superseded by a merged PR, or grown a discussion that reveals hidden complexity. The label becomes maintained rather than decorative.

The wider point this is making: onboarding docs go stale because they're written once. An agent that reads the current code can regenerate the answer each time it's asked, which is a different model of documentation entirely.

### Rough effort

M — one hackathon day

### Are you planning to build this yourself?

Maybe — happy to team up with someone

### Team name

_(unclaimed)_

### Anything else?

- Good repo to test against: any large OSS project with a crowded `good first issue` list. Measuring how many are actually stale would be a strong opening slide.
- Careful with tone in the generated ramp-up notes — condescending onboarding is worse than none.
- Stretch: after a first PR merges, suggest the natural next issue, so there's a path rather than a single step.
title: [Idea] First-issue matchmaker — ranked good first issues plus generated ramp-up notes

> [!NOTE]
> **Example issue, seeded by the organizers.** It shows roughly the level of detail we're hoping for — yours can be shorter. Please don't edit or claim this one; [submit your own idea](../../issues/new?template=1-challenge-idea.yml) instead.

### The idea in one or two sentences

A daily plain-language digest of what actually moved on a project board, delivered as text — readable in a screen reader, an email, a terminal, or a Slack message, with no drag-and-drop and no colour-coding required.

### What problem does it solve?

Project boards are intensely visual. Meaning is carried by column position, by card colour, by where something sits relative to something else. That works well right up until it doesn't:

- A screen reader user has to traverse a grid to answer "what changed since yesterday?"
- Someone on a phone on a train gets a horizontally scrolling board with eight columns.
- Anyone who thinks in prose rather than in kanban has to reconstruct the story every morning.

And there's a newer version of this problem. When agents are moving cards too, the board changes while nobody is watching it, so "what changed overnight" becomes a real question rather than a rhetorical one.

### Theme

Accessibility & inclusion (collaboration that works for everyone)

### Where does the "agentic" part come in?

A raw changelog isn't the answer — "17 items changed status" is technically accurate and completely useless. An agent takes the diff of the board between two points in time and writes what a good teammate would say out loud:

> Yesterday the automation theme moved. Three of the four sub-issues under #42 are done, all closed by the coding agent, and the last one is blocked on a review that's been sitting for two days. Nothing else moved. #57 is still unclaimed after four days — it may be too vague to pick up.

Note what that includes: not just movement, but **absence** of movement, and a guess at why. Stalls are the thing boards hide best and the thing digests can surface cheaply.

Output should be genuinely plain: no tables, no emoji load-bearing anything, semantic headings, and every issue referenced by number and title so it's navigable.

### Rough effort

S — a few hours

### Are you planning to build this yourself?

No — I'm donating it, any team may take it

### Team name

_(donated — unclaimed)_

### Anything else?

- Scheduled Action + GraphQL query for items updated in the last 24h is the whole data layer.
- Test it properly: run the output through VoiceOver or NVDA before you demo. If it's only *theoretically* accessible, it isn't.
- Stretch: `/digest last week` on demand, and a per-team filter.
- A nice side effect — a plain-text board summary is also exactly the format another agent wants to consume as context.
title: [Idea] Plain-text daily board digest for screen readers and low bandwidth

> [!NOTE]
> **Example issue, seeded by the organizers.** It shows roughly the level of detail we're hoping for — yours can be shorter. Please don't edit or claim this one; [submit your own idea](../../issues/new?template=1-challenge-idea.yml) instead.

### The idea in one or two sentences

Comment `/split` on a big vague issue and an agent decomposes it into linked sub-issues, works out which ones are mechanical, and hands *those* to the Copilot coding agent — leaving the judgement-heavy ones for the humans.

### What problem does it solve?

Big issues sit still. "Migrate the settings page to the new design system" is real work, but it's not *startable* — so it drifts across three sprints while everyone picks off smaller things around it. The fix has always been "break it down", and breaking it down is tedious enough that people put it off.

There's a second problem sitting underneath. Inside that big issue, maybe 60% is mechanical — rename these props, update these imports, regenerate these snapshots — and 40% needs taste. Right now those are welded together in one ticket, so a human does all of it, including the boring parts an agent would happily do.

### Theme

Automation (Actions, webhooks, bots, the GraphQL API)

### Where does the "agentic" part come in?

Three passes, each with a different level of trust:

1. **Decompose.** The agent reads the issue and any linked code, proposes 3–8 sub-issues, and creates them as real sub-issues so the parent gets a progress bar for free.
2. **Classify.** Each sub-issue is tagged mechanical or judgement. Mechanical means: the outcome is fully determined by the description, and a diff can be verified without opinion.
3. **Delegate.** Mechanical sub-issues get assigned to the Copilot coding agent. Judgement ones stay unassigned for humans to claim.

The classify step is the risky one, and being wrong there is exactly the interesting failure. An agent that assigns itself a design decision produces a confident, wrong PR. So it should be biased heavily toward "judgement" when unsure, and every classification should be visible and one click to override.

The thing this is really testing: can a team's board become a *dispatcher* between human and machine work, rather than just a list?

### Rough effort

L — full hackathon

### Are you planning to build this yourself?

Yes — my team is claiming it

### Team name

Team Example (organizers)

### Anything else?

- Sub-issues are first-class in the GraphQL API, so the parent/child progress rollup comes for free — worth building on rather than faking with checklists.
- Guard rail worth adding: cap it at 8 sub-issues. Unbounded decomposition produces 30 tickets and despair.
- Demo idea: run `/split` live on a deliberately vague issue, then show the board grouped by assignee with the mechanical items already in flight.
title: [Idea] /split — decompose an epic into sub-issues and route the mechanical ones to Copilot

> [!NOTE]
> **Example issue, seeded by the organizers.** It shows roughly the level of detail we're hoping for — yours can be shorter. Please don't edit or claim this one; [submit your own idea](../../issues/new?template=1-challenge-idea.yml) instead.

### The idea in one or two sentences

A bot that scores every new issue for **agent-readiness** and leaves one concrete suggestion for making it better — a "definition of ready" linter, for a world where the next reader might be a machine.

### What problem does it solve?

"Fix the login bug" was always a bad issue. It used to be survivable, because a human would wander over and ask what you meant. Hand the same issue to a coding agent and it will confidently build the wrong thing, open a PR, and cost you more time than writing the issue properly would have.

So issue quality stopped being a nice-to-have and became the actual bottleneck. But nobody wants to enforce it with a 12-field template that makes people give up halfway through.

### Theme

Planning & tracking (Issues, Projects, milestones, roadmaps)

### Where does the "agentic" part come in?

An agent reads each new issue and judges whether *it* could act on it — the model is the rubric, rather than a regex checklist. It scores four things:

| Signal | Rough question |
| --- | --- |
| Observable outcome | Would you know when this is done? |
| Scope | Is this one change or five? |
| Context | Are the files, repo, or reproduction steps identified? |
| Ambiguity | Are there undefined terms doing heavy lifting? |

Then it posts **one** comment with a score out of 4 and a single suggested rewrite of the weakest part. Not a wall of feedback — one thing.

Two design details that matter more than the scoring:

- **It never blocks.** A linter that stops you filing an issue means people stop filing issues.
- **It's honest about itself.** If the agent can't score the issue confidently, it says so instead of inventing a number.

Stretch: issues scoring 4/4 get an `agent-ready` label, and the board grows a view of work that could be safely handed to Copilot right now.

### Rough effort

S — a few hours

### Are you planning to build this yourself?

No — I'm donating it, any team may take it

### Team name

_(donated — unclaimed)_

### Anything else?

- Genuinely doable in an afternoon: `issues.opened` workflow, one model call, one `gh issue comment`.
- Good demo: run it over this repo's own issue history and show the score distribution.
- Interesting thing to measure if you have time — do issues that scored 4/4 actually get resolved faster? If not, the rubric is wrong, and that's a more interesting finding than the tool.
title: [Idea] Agent-readiness linter — a 'definition of ready' bot for issues

> [!NOTE]
> **Example issue, seeded by the organizers.** It shows roughly the level of detail we're hoping for — yours can be shorter. Please don't edit or claim this one; [submit your own idea](../../issues/new?template=1-challenge-idea.yml) instead.

### The idea in one or two sentences

A dashboard that answers a question no team can currently answer: **on this project board, which work was moved by a human and which was moved by an agent?** Same charts, split by who did it.

### What problem does it solve?

Teams are quietly handing more and more work to coding agents, and they have no idea how much. Ask a team "what percentage of your closed issues last month were finished by an agent?" and you'll get a shrug and a guess. That's a problem in both directions: you can't tell where agents are genuinely carrying load, and you can't tell where they're producing churn that a human silently cleans up afterwards.

Velocity charts still assume one kind of contributor. That assumption quietly broke.

### Theme

Insights & metrics (dashboards, reporting, project analytics)

### Where does the "agentic" part come in?

Two layers.

**Measuring agents.** Project item events and issue timelines tell you who moved each item and when. Bot accounts and the coding agent are identifiable, so you can attribute every status change, every comment, every PR. From that you get: throughput split by actor type, time-in-status split by actor type, and the one everyone will actually stare at — *rework rate*, meaning how often an agent-closed item gets reopened or immediately follow-up-PR'd by a human.

**Agent doing the analysis.** The numbers on their own invite bad conclusions. A second pass has an agent write the narrative: "agent throughput on `theme: automation` is 3× human, but rework is 40% — the wins are concentrated in mechanical refactors." Chart plus caveat, rather than chart alone.

### Rough effort

M — one hackathon day

### Are you planning to build this yourself?

Maybe — happy to team up with someone

### Team name

_(unclaimed — looking for a teammate who likes data viz)_

### Anything else?

- Everything needed is in the GraphQL API: project item field-value history, `IssueTimelineItems`, and PR authorship.
- Watch out for the `github-actions[bot]` vs. Copilot vs. genuine human distinction — some humans commit through automation, which will skew things if you don't handle it.
- Doesn't need a backend. A static page reading a nightly JSON dump written by an Action would demo perfectly well.
- The honest failure mode to look for: rework rate might turn out to be *low* and boring, in which case the interesting finding is "agents are fine and nobody noticed."
title: [Idea] Human vs. agent contribution dashboard for a project board

> [!NOTE]
> **Example issue, seeded by the organizers.** It shows roughly the level of detail we're hoping for — yours can be shorter. Please don't edit or claim this one; [submit your own idea](../../issues/new?template=1-challenge-idea.yml) instead.

### The idea in one or two sentences

A "Scribe" agent that watches a Discussion thread and turns the messy conversation into a set of properly scoped issues — each with a title, acceptance criteria, a theme label, and a rough estimate — for a human to approve in a single review.

### What problem does it solve?

Every planning conversation ends the same way: forty messages of good thinking, and then someone has to sit down and turn it into issues. It takes about half an hour, it's nobody's favourite job, and it's the first thing that gets skipped when the week is busy. When it does get done, the issues are inconsistent — some have acceptance criteria, some are two words long — which means the next person (or agent) picking one up has to go re-read the original thread anyway.

The information was all there in the conversation. It just never made it into a trackable shape.

### Theme

Agentic workflows (Copilot coding agent, AI-assisted planning and triage)

### Where does the "agentic" part come in?

The agent does the drafting, the human does the deciding.

On a `/scribe` comment in a Discussion, the agent:

1. Reads the whole thread, including reactions — heavily 👍'd suggestions get weighted higher.
2. Clusters the conversation into candidate work items and drops anything that reads as an aside.
3. Drafts each one with a title, a two-line summary, acceptance criteria, a theme label, and an S/M/L estimate.
4. Posts them **as a single preview comment**, not as issues.

A human then replies with which ones to keep. Only then does the agent open the issues, add them to the board, and link them back to the source Discussion.

The preview step is the whole design. An agent that silently opens fourteen issues is worse than no agent — you've replaced half an hour of writing with an hour of cleanup. The interesting question this idea is really poking at is *where the human checkpoint belongs*, and "draft everything, commit nothing" is our guess at the answer.

### Rough effort

M — one hackathon day

### Are you planning to build this yourself?

No — I'm donating it, any team may take it

### Team name

_(donated — unclaimed)_

### Anything else?

- The GraphQL API can read Discussions (`repository.discussion.comments`) and create issues, so no scraping needed.
- Stretch goal: after the issues exist, have the agent link them as sub-issues under a parent tracking issue.
- Nice demo moment: paste a real, genuinely rambling planning thread and show the preview it produces.
title: [Idea] Scribe — turn a Discussion thread into scoped, agent-ready issues
